root.note: The word is pre-Roman and points to the Basque word, but the d of izquierda and its presence in Portuguese are not explained. One etymologist calls it an unsolved mystery.

stages.meaning: left (a la izquierda: on the left)

history: Derecha, ‘right’, is a Latin word. Izquierda isn't. Latin had sinister, which gave Spanish siniestra, but a word from before the Romans pushed it out. Dictionaries point to Basque ezker, ‘left’, and the first Castilian records are exquerdo in 1117 and izquierdo in 1142. Catalan esquerra and Portuguese esquerda belong to the same group. The details remain unsolved: the d in Spanish and Portuguese has no clear source, and Portuguese has no Basque background. Corominas proposed esku ‘hand’ + oker ‘twisted’, but this is only a theory. The political left is newer. It goes back to 1789, when opponents of the king's veto sat on the left of the French Assembly.
historyEinfach: Most Spanish words come from Latin, but izquierda does not. It is older than the Romans in Spain. It is probably connected to the Basque word ezker, ‘left’. Experts still discuss the details. The old Latin word was sinister. Spanish lost it. Catalan and Portuguese have words like izquierda too.

elsewhere.text: Portuguese has the word with the same d as Spanish. It is one of the puzzles, because Portuguese never had a Basque-speaking background.
